title: From Empty Wall to Broadway: Andrew Lloyd Webber Plans a Musical About the 1911 Mona Lisa Heist
summary:
Picture the most recognizable painting on Earth—Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa—hanging in the Louvre, behind protective glass, adored by millions. Now picture an empty wall where it used to be. That surreal scene unfolded on August 22, 1911, when a museum artist arrived to sketch the portrait and found only four bare hooks. The Mona Lisa had been stolen, and it would remain missing for over two years. Now, Andrew Lloyd Webber, the composer behind legendary spectacles like The Phantom of the Opera and Cats, is turning this stranger-than-fiction tale into a musical.

Lloyd Webber, whose shows are known for their fever-dream imagery—a subterranean lake, a tribe of singing cats, a pharaoh with Elvis-style vibrato—announced the project almost as an afterthought following the premiere of Cats: The Jellicle Ball on Broadway. "It's a true story about how the Mona Lisa disappeared... and ended up in Italy," he teased, offering no further details. But the historical record is rich with drama.

In the early 1900s, the Mona Lisa was already receiving fan mail—yes, love letters addressed to a painting—so the Louvre decided to encase it in glass. One of the workers hired for the job was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian glazier and housepainter. As author R.A. Scotti noted, "Since he had put her in the frame, he knew better than anyone how to remove her." On August 21, 1911, a Monday when the museum was closed, Peruggia—possibly with accomplices—donned a worker's smock, lifted the 30-inch-tall panel from its case, and carried it to a stairwell. There, he separated the painting from its heavy frame and walked out.

The theft went unnoticed for 28 hours. When the alarm was finally raised, the Louvre's director initially assumed the painting was merely being photographed. Police pursued numerous false leads, even briefly suspecting Pablo Picasso. They interviewed Peruggia at his apartment—where the masterpiece was stashed in a trunk—but he didn't arouse suspicion. For two years, the trail went cold. Then, in late 1913, Peruggia contacted an art dealer in Florence, demanding a ransom. The dealer alerted authorities, and Peruggia was arrested. His motive? He claimed he wanted to return the painting to Italy, arguing that "it seems to belong to Italy since its painter was an Italian." Many Italians hailed him as a patriot, and he embraced the role.

The heist transformed the Mona Lisa into a global sensation. Before the theft, it wasn't even the most famous painting in its gallery. But as news spread, thousands flocked to the Louvre just to stare at the blank wall. Lloyd Webber, who has a knack for finding the spectacular in the strange, now has a story that blends art, obsession, and a bumbling caper—perfect fodder for a musical that will likely be anything but a quiet portrait.
why_it_matters: The Mona Lisa's transformation from a respected portrait to a worldwide icon shows how a single event can reshape cultural value. For a 12-to-14-year-old, this story reveals that even masterpieces have unpredictable histories—and that fame often depends on dramatic moments, not just artistic merit.

background_read: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa in the early 1500s, but it was not instantly world-famous. It gained prestige slowly, in part because it was owned by French kings and later placed in the Louvre Museum (the world's largest art museum, in Paris). Before the 1911 theft, it was respected but not the most celebrated portrait; that changed when newspapers across the globe covered the heist.

Andrew Lloyd Webber, the British composer behind this planned musical, is famous for extravagant Broadway productions like Cats, The Phantom of the Opera, and Evita. His style often mixes historical oddities with spectacular staging—perfect for a real-life art caper. The story's central figure, Vincenzo Peruggia, is a classic example of an unlikely thief whose patriotic claims divided public opinion, some seeing him as a hero and others as a common criminal.

The heist also intersected with the art world's elite: police briefly suspected Pablo Picasso, the Spanish painter who co-founded Cubism, though he was innocent. The case shows how crime, art, and nationalism can merge into a narrative that continues to fascinate more than a century later.

perspectives.description: Fans of Lloyd Webber and the original heist story may see the musical as a thrilling tribute to art history. It brings a forgotten, stranger-than-fiction episode to a new audience, highlighting how museums and cultural treasures can captivate the public imagination. The project also offers an entertaining way to teach about legacy, ambition, and the blurred line between heroism and crime.

Critics might worry that turning a historical theft into a musical trivializes the serious breach of a museum's security and the violation of artistic integrity. Peruggia's patriotic justification, however flawed, risks being romanticized on stage while ignoring the ethical and legal questions of taking what does not belong to you. Some art historians may feel that the painting's true value is overshadowed by a sensationalized caper.

Historically, art heists have often boosted the mystique of the stolen objects—the Mona Lisa is only the most famous example. This pattern reveals how public attention often follows disruption rather than stable appreciation. The musical, therefore, fits a long tradition of using crime as a narrative hook to explore deeper questions about ownership, identity, and what makes an artwork 'priceless.'

If successful, this musical could spark renewed interest in historical heists and the stories behind museum collections. It might inspire other artists to mine forgotten episodes for contemporary works. However, it also raises questions about how we represent complex figures like Peruggia—do we turn criminals into sympathetic characters, and what consequences does that carry for our understanding of justice and heritage?
